title: What is disaster recovery on AWS — the four strategies from cheapest to fastest: Backup & Restore (hours to recover), Pilot Light (keep minimum resources running, scale up on disaster), Warm Standby (scaled-down copy always running), Multi-Site Active-Active (full copy in another region, instant failover) — and what is RPO (how much data you can lose) vs RTO (how long you can be down)?
shortTitle: Disaster Recovery on AWS — Four Strategies, RPO and RTO

s1_definition.profdef: Disaster recovery (DR) on AWS is the set of strategies for restoring a workload in another location after a major failure, and there are four, ordered from cheapest and slowest to most expensive and fastest. Backup & Restore keeps backups and rebuilds the environment on disaster, recovering in hours. Pilot Light keeps a minimal core (such as a replicated database) always running and scales up the rest on disaster. Warm Standby runs a scaled-down but fully functional copy continuously that you scale up on failover. Multi-Site Active-Active runs full capacity in multiple Regions serving live traffic, giving near-instant failover. RPO, Recovery Point Objective, is how much data you can afford to lose, measured as a time window; RTO, Recovery Time Objective, is how long you can afford to be down before recovery.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India must survive its main building being destroyed. Backup & Restore is keeping copies of all records in a warehouse and, if disaster strikes, renting a new building and setting everything up from scratch — cheap to maintain, but it takes hours to reopen. Pilot Light is keeping just the vault and the core ledger mirrored in a second building, lights off, ready to switch on and furnish quickly. Warm Standby is a smaller, fully working branch in a second city, open with a few staff, that you rapidly scale up if the main branch fails. Multi-Site Active-Active is two full branches in two cities, both serving customers right now, so if one is destroyed the other simply keeps going. RPO is "how many minutes of transactions can we afford to lose?" and RTO is "how many minutes can we be closed?"
s1_definition.oneliner: DR runs from cheap-and-slow to costly-and-instant — Backup & Restore, Pilot Light, Warm Standby, Multi-Site Active-Active — and you pick based on RPO, how much data you can lose, and RTO, how long you can be down.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Disaster recovery (DR) on AWS is the set of strategies for restoring a workload in another location after a major failure, and there are four, ordered from cheapest and slowest to most expensive and fastest. Backup & Restore keeps backups and rebuilds the environment on disaster, recovering in hours. Pilot Light keeps a minimal core (such as a replicated database) always running and scales up the rest on disaster. Warm Standby runs a scaled-down but fully functional copy continuously that you scale up on failover. Multi-Site Active-Active runs full capacity in multiple Regions serving live traffic, giving near-instant failover. RPO, Recovery Point Objective, is how much data you can afford to lose, measured as a time window; RTO, Recovery Time Objective, is how long you can afford to be down before recovery.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India must survive its main building being destroyed. Backup & Restore is keeping copies of all records in a warehouse and, if disaster strikes, renting a new building and setting everything up from scratch — cheap to maintain, but it takes hours to reopen. Pilot Light is keeping just the vault and the core ledger mirrored in a second building, lights off, ready to switch on and furnish quickly. Warm Standby is a smaller, fully working branch in a second city, open with a few staff, that you rapidly scale up if the main branch fails. Multi-Site Active-Active is two full branches in two cities, both serving customers right now, so if one is destroyed the other simply keeps going. RPO is "how many minutes of transactions can we afford to lose?" and RTO is "how many minutes can we be closed?"

**One line to remember:** DR runs from cheap-and-slow to costly-and-instant — Backup & Restore, Pilot Light, Warm Standby, Multi-Site Active-Active — and you pick based on RPO, how much data you can lose, and RTO, how long you can be down.

sections.s2_technical:
Disaster recovery is about surviving a loss big enough that your primary environment is unavailable — an Availability Zone or even a whole Region. The four strategies trade cost against speed of recovery, and you choose by your RPO and RTO targets.

RPO, the Recovery Point Objective, answers how much data you can lose. If your RPO is five minutes, you must be able to recover to a state no more than five minutes before the disaster, which demands frequent or continuous replication. RTO, the Recovery Time Objective, answers how long you can be down. If your RTO is ten minutes, the whole failover must complete within ten minutes. Tighter objectives cost more.

```java
// DR targets drive the strategy choice.
record DrTargets(int rpoMinutes, int rtoMinutes) {}
DrTargets coreLedger = new DrTargets(1, 5);   // almost no data loss, fast recovery
DrTargets internalReport = new DrTargets(1440, 240); // a day of data, hours down OK
```

Backup & Restore is the cheapest. You take regular backups — EBS snapshots, RDS snapshots, S3 copies, often to another Region — and on disaster you provision infrastructure (ideally from infrastructure-as-code) and restore from backup. RPO equals your backup frequency and RTO is hours because you rebuild from nothing. It suits workloads that can tolerate being down for hours and losing some data.

Pilot Light keeps the critical core always running in the recovery Region, typically a continuously replicated database, while the application tier exists only as configuration or stopped resources. On disaster you start and scale the application tier and point traffic over. Because the data is already there, RPO is small (seconds to minutes), and RTO is shorter than Backup & Restore because you only start the app, not rebuild everything.

Warm Standby runs a scaled-down but fully working copy of the whole stack in the recovery Region all the time, handling no or little traffic. On disaster you scale it up to full capacity and shift traffic. RPO is small and RTO is minutes, because the system is already running and just needs to grow. It costs more because you always pay for the standby.

Multi-Site Active-Active runs full capacity in two or more Regions, all serving live traffic, usually with data replicated both ways or a globally distributed database. If a Region fails, the others absorb its traffic almost instantly, so RPO is near zero and RTO is near zero. It is the most expensive and the most complex, because you must handle data consistency across Regions.

A senior nuance: you do not pick one strategy for the whole company; you pick per workload based on its business criticality. The core payment ledger might justify Warm Standby or Active-Active, while an internal analytics dashboard is fine on Backup & Restore. And a DR plan is worthless unless you test the failover regularly, because untested recovery procedures fail exactly when you need them. AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery and cross-Region replication features help implement these patterns.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India must keep operating even if its primary Region fails. Different systems have different tolerances: the core payment ledger can lose almost no data and can be down only minutes, while an internal report can lose a day of data and be down for hours. Using one DR strategy for both would either overspend on the report or under-protect the ledger. This is exactly what choosing a DR strategy per workload, driven by RPO and RTO, solves.

Problem 2 — The team must know, for a given RPO and RTO, which strategy is appropriate and roughly what it costs. This is exactly what a DR advisor provides.

We will write a small DR advisor. `DrTargets` holds RPO and RTO in minutes. `DrAdvisor` recommends one of the four strategies and estimates relative cost. The demo evaluates the core ledger, a customer-facing API, and an internal report, showing how tighter targets push toward costlier, faster strategies.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three workloads with different RPO and RTO targets — the core payment ledger (one minute, five minutes), the customer API (five minutes, thirty minutes), and an internal report (one day, four hours).

Step 1. The core payment ledger is evaluated. Its RPO of one minute and RTO of five minutes are extremely tight, meaning almost no data loss and near-instant recovery, so the advisor recommends Multi-Site Active-Active and flags it as the highest cost. Only a full live copy in another Region can meet such tight targets.

Step 2. The customer API is evaluated. It can tolerate five minutes of data loss and thirty minutes of downtime, so the advisor recommends Warm Standby, a scaled-down live copy that is scaled up on failover, at high but not maximum cost.

Step 3. The internal report is evaluated. It can lose a whole day of data and be down for four hours, so the advisor recommends Backup & Restore, the cheapest strategy, because rebuilding from backups within hours is perfectly acceptable here.

Step 4. The results show the principle clearly: as the RPO and RTO targets get tighter, the recommended strategy moves up the ladder toward faster and more expensive options, and as they relax, it moves down toward cheaper ones.

Step 5. The final output logs each workload with its targets, the recommended strategy, and the relative cost, giving the team a per-workload DR plan rather than one blanket choice.

```
2026-10-29 02:55:00 [INFO] core-payment-ledger (RPO 1m, RTO 5m) -> Multi-Site Active-Active (near-zero RPO/RTO, full copy in another region) [cost $$$$ highest]
2026-10-29 02:55:00 [INFO] customer-api (RPO 5m, RTO 30m) -> Warm Standby (scaled-down copy always running, scale up on failover) [cost $$$ high]
2026-10-29 02:55:00 [INFO] internal-report (RPO 1440m, RTO 240m) -> Backup & Restore (rebuild from backups, recover in hours) [cost $ lowest]
```

```
  │ full copy LIVE   │ RTO minutes  │ RTO <2h      │ RTO hours        │

```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Disaster recovery on AWS is how I restore a workload in another location after a failure large enough to take out the primary environment, and there are four strategies that trade cost against recovery speed. I choose between them using two numbers: RPO, the Recovery Point Objective, which is how much data I can afford to lose, expressed as a time window, and RTO, the Recovery Time Objective, which is how long I can afford to be down. Tighter objectives always cost more.

From cheapest and slowest to most expensive and fastest, the four are these. Backup & Restore keeps backups and rebuilds the environment from scratch on disaster, so the RPO equals the backup frequency and the RTO is hours; it suits workloads that can tolerate being down and losing some data. Pilot Light keeps the critical core, usually a continuously replicated database, always running in the recovery Region while the application tier is dormant, so the data is current and recovery is faster because I only start and scale the app. Warm Standby runs a scaled-down but fully working copy of the whole stack all the time and scales it up on failover, giving a small RPO and an RTO of minutes. Multi-Site Active-Active runs full capacity in multiple Regions all serving live traffic, so if one Region fails the others absorb it almost instantly, giving near-zero RPO and RTO, at the highest cost and complexity.

The senior point I always make is that you do not pick one strategy for the whole organization — you pick per workload by its business criticality, and a DR plan is worthless unless you actually test the failover regularly, because untested recovery fails exactly when you need it.

At National Bank of India I applied this per workload. The core payment ledger had an RPO of about a minute and an RTO of a few minutes, which only Multi-Site Active-Active across two Regions with a globally replicated database could meet, so we paid for that. The customer-facing API, which could tolerate a little data loss and about thirty minutes of downtime, ran on Warm Standby — a scaled-down live copy we scaled up on failover. And internal reporting, which could lose a day of data and be down for hours, stayed on cheap Backup & Restore. We ran game-day failover drills on a schedule to prove the RTO and RPO were real, because I have seen untested DR plans quietly rot until the day they are needed and then fail.
